texts.0: SP, due to reliance on memory instead of the printed check list, did not execute all checks according to check list in a standardized manner. SP omitted four items across the Before Start and Before Taxi checks, including one that affected the avionics configuration for the instrument sortie. The IP intervened, stopped the flow and re-ran both checks from the top before taxi was authorized.
texts.1: SP, due to reliance on memory instead of the printed check list, did not execute the checks in the sequence and wording required by the check list. SP omitted two items and had to be told item by item what remained outstanding, with the flow restarted only after three verbal prompts from the IP. The checks were finally completed correctly, but only through IP direction and with a delay of about two minutes on the planned start time.
texts.2: SP, due to a rushed challenge-and-response rhythm on the ground checks, did not read and confirm every line of the check list before moving on. SP skipped one item in the Before Taxi flow, recognized the gap while still stationary and re-ran the affected section without prompting. No IP intervention or prompting was required and the departure time was unaffected.
texts.3: SP executed all checks according to check list, in sequence and without omissions, and did not skip any procedure of LAP or SOPs. Each item was challenged and confirmed against the actual switch or indication before SP moved to the next line. The full ground flow was completed without any IP intervention and within the planned timeline.
texts.4: SP executed the complete ground check list flow in an impeccable and standardized manner, with every item verified against the corresponding indication. SP kept the challenge-and-response discipline unchanged under the added workload of the instrument avionics setup. No omission, no repetition and no IP input of any kind were required at any point.
texts.marginal: SP executed all checks according to check list and skipped no procedure, so the ground flow met the standard. However, SP's pace was uneven, with two items read back only after a visible pause to locate the corresponding switch, which leaves little margin on a compressed turnaround. SP is expected to consolidate the switch positions by memory location so that the check list is used for confirmation rather than for search.

texts_at.0: With the IP reading each checklist line aloud and pointing to the switch or indication in turn, SP responded to the challenge and moved to the next item on the IP's pace. The printed sequence and wording of the check list have not yet been learned well enough to set the pace independently, so the flow is still paced from memory rather than from the page. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin reading and confirming each line directly from the check list without the pace being set by the IP.
texts_at.1: SP completed the checklist flow with one item actioned only after a verbal reminder from the IP, because the challenge-and-response pace was being set from memory rather than from the printed page. Every other item was read, challenged and confirmed correctly once the reminder had been given. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to reduce reliance on the verbal reminder as the checklist sequence becomes more familiar.
texts_at.2: SP skipped one item in the Before Taxi flow and corrected it without prompting, recognizing the gap while still stationary rather than needing the IP to point it out. The rushed challenge-and-response rhythm that produced the gap did not affect the departure time. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to slow the challenge-and-response rhythm so no item needs to be caught after the fact.
texts_at.3: SP executed all checks according to check list, in sequence and without omissions, working each line against the actual switch or indication before moving on. The read-back tempo quickened slightly toward the end of the Before Taxi checks, though every item was still confirmed correctly. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold an even tempo through to the last item of the flow.

texts_above.1: SP worked through the checklist flow, completing every item correctly. The correction followed a verbal reminder from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP skipped no item across the Before Start and Before Taxi checks and caught a slowed rhythm at one point before it produced an omission, without any prompting from the IP. The recovery cost only a few seconds and left the timeline for taxi unaffected. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good challenge-and-response discipline.
texts_above.3: SP worked every item of the ground flow against the actual switch or indication in a single unbroken pass, with no item requiring a second look. The Before Start and Before Taxi checks ran at a constant, deliberate pace despite the added avionics setup for the instrument sortie. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed challenge-and-response discipline.
texts_above.4: SP ran the complete ground check list flow without a single repeated item, a dropped tempo or a moment of searching for a switch, holding the challenge-and-response rhythm unchanged from Before Start through Before Taxi. The IP had nothing to add at any point in the sequence. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent challenge-and-response discipline.

error_modes.label: AIRCRAFT CONDITION ASSESSMENT AND FLIGHT PERMISSIBILITY DECISION

texts.0: SP, due to mission-completion bias in pressing on past the briefed decision point, did not specify the A/C condition correctly and did not decide its flight permissibility on the basis of the aircraft forms. SP accepted an open write-up affecting a navigation aid required for the planned instrument profile and declared the aircraft serviceable. The IP intervened, stopped the acceptance and directed a return to maintenance before start.
texts.1: SP, due to mission-completion bias in pressing on past the briefed decision point, did not review the aircraft forms fully before deciding on flight permissibility. SP declared the aircraft acceptable and revised that decision only after two direct questions from the IP about the open write-up and its effect on the instrument sortie. The final decision was correct but reached through IP prompting rather than through SP's own assessment.
texts.2: SP, due to a partial first pass through the aircraft forms, did not immediately relate an open write-up to the requirements of the planned instrument profile. SP re-opened the forms before walk-around, identified the entry and confirmed with maintenance that the affected system was serviceable for the sortie. The decision on flight permissibility was reached without IP intervention and without delay to the start.
texts.3: SP specified the A/C condition correctly and decided its flight permissibility confidently, on the basis of a complete review of the aircraft forms and the walk-around findings. SP related each open entry to the navigation equipment required for the instrument profile and stated the conclusion without hesitation. No IP input was needed at any stage of the assessment.
texts.4: SP specified the A/C condition and decided its flight permissibility correctly, confidently and without a single re-check being required. SP identified the one open write-up in the forms, stated precisely which system it affected and confirmed that the instrument profile as briefed remained flyable. The assessment was complete, accurate and delivered before the IP had asked for it.
texts.marginal: SP specified the A/C condition correctly and the decision on flight permissibility was sound, so the standard was met. However, SP stated the conclusion only after a second pass through the forms and phrased it tentatively, which indicates the assessment is not yet confident. SP is expected to consolidate the forms review into one deliberate pass and to state the flight permissibility decision without qualification.

texts_at.0: With the IP walking through the aircraft forms line by line and pointing out any open write-up, SP reviewed the entries on the IP's lead. The habit of relating an open write-up to the planned profile has not yet been built, so the review is still guided rather than completed independently. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin relating each open entry to the planned profile without it being pointed out.
texts_at.1: SP reached the correct flight-permissibility decision only after two direct questions from the IP about the open write-up, because the first pass through the aircraft forms had not connected the entry to the instrument profile. Once prompted, SP related the entry to the navigation equipment required and confirmed the aircraft was flyable. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to make that connection unprompted on the next review of the forms.
texts_at.2: SP related the open write-up to the instrument profile and confirmed the affected system was serviceable without the IP raising it, after a first pass through the forms that had missed the connection. The re-check was completed before walk-around with no delay to the start. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to make the connection on the first pass so the forms need only one review.
texts_at.3: SP specified the A/C condition correctly and reached the flight-permissibility decision on a complete review of the forms and the walk-around findings. The conclusion was reached only after a second look at the open entry, rather than being stated on the first pass. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to state the conclusion after a single deliberate pass through the forms.

texts_above.1: SP reached the correct flight-permissibility decision, relating the open write-up to its effect on the instrument sortie. The correction followed two direct questions from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP related the open write-up to the instrument profile on review of the aircraft forms and confirmed the affected navigation equipment was serviceable, reaching the decision without any IP input. The conclusion was stated clearly once the entry had been checked against the flight plan. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound aircraft-forms review.
texts_above.3: SP reviewed the aircraft forms and the walk-around findings as one pass, related the open entry to the navigation equipment the instrument profile required and stated the flight-permissibility decision without hesitation. No part of the assessment needed a second look. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate aircraft-forms review.
texts_above.4: SP identified the one open write-up, stated precisely which system it affected and confirmed the instrument profile as briefed remained flyable, delivering the assessment before the IP had asked for it. The decision was complete, accurate and unqualified. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate aircraft-forms review.

error_modes.label: GROUND CREW COORDINATION AND CLEARANCE BEFORE SWITCH OR CONTROL MOVEMENT

texts.0: SP, due to inadequate crew coordination between front and rear cockpit, did not confirm the ground crew's position before activating switches and moving the A/C controls. SP ran the flight control check with a marshaller still inside the wing arc and gave no hand signal in either direction. The IP intervened, halted the check and had the area cleared before the flow was resumed.
texts.1: SP, due to inadequate crew coordination between front and rear cockpit, did not establish a clear exchange with the ground crew before activating the electrical switches. SP began the sequence without a signal, and it was stopped and re-sequenced only after two verbal prompts from the IP to confirm that the crew was clear. Coordination was eventually correct but was driven entirely by IP direction.
texts.2: SP, due to a hand signal given before eye contact with the marshaller was established, did not ensure that the ground crew had acknowledged the intended action. SP recognized the missing acknowledgement, held the switch action, repeated the signal and proceeded only after a clear response. Cooperation with ground crew continued without mis-apprehensions and without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP cooperated with the ground crew without allowing mis-apprehensions and confirmed their position before activating any switch or moving any A/C controls. Each signal was given, acknowledged and answered before the corresponding action was taken. The whole start and pre-taxi sequence was completed without IP intervention.
texts.4: SP cooperated with the ground crew throughout with unambiguous, correctly timed signals, and verified their position visually before every switch activation and control movement. SP anticipated the marshaller's requirements at each step, so no signal had to be repeated or clarified. The exchange was complete, standard and free of any mis-apprehension.
texts.marginal: SP cooperated with the ground crew without mis-apprehensions and confirmed their position before acting, so the standard was met. However, two signals were given while SP's attention was still inside the cockpit, and the acknowledgement was obtained only on the second look outside. SP is expected to complete the visual clearance check before initiating the signal, so that the confirmation precedes rather than follows the action.

texts_at.0: With the IP demonstrating the hand signal and confirming the ground crew's position before each switch, SP activated the switches on the IP's cue. The sequence of signal, acknowledgement and action has not yet been learned, so switches are still activated once the IP has confirmed the exchange rather than by SP's own check. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to begin confirming the ground crew's position independently before each switch is activated.
texts_at.1: SP completed the ground crew coordination only after two verbal prompts from the IP to confirm the crew was clear, because the exchange had begun without a signal. The sequence was then re-run correctly and the crew's position was confirmed before any further switch was activated. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to open the exchange with a signal before the IP needs to prompt it.
texts_at.2: SP recognized a hand signal given before eye contact was established, held the switch action, repeated the signal and proceeded only once a clear response was seen. No IP intervention was needed and no mis-apprehension carried into the next step. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to establish eye contact before the signal so the repeat is no longer necessary.
texts_at.3: SP cooperated with the ground crew without mis-apprehensions and confirmed their position before every switch activation and control movement, with each signal given, acknowledged and answered in turn. Two of the signals were given while attention was still partly inside the cockpit, though acknowledgement was obtained before acting. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to complete the outside scan before initiating each signal.

texts_above.1: SP completed the ground crew coordination sequence correctly, confirming the crew was clear before activating the electrical switches. The correction followed two verbal prompts from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP confirmed the ground crew's position and exchanged a clear signal before every switch activation, with one signal repeated on SP's own initiative when the first acknowledgement was uncertain. Cooperation continued without mis-apprehension and without any IP input. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid ground-crew signal coordination.
texts_above.3: SP gave, had acknowledged and answered every signal to the ground crew before the corresponding action was taken, with the visual clearance completed ahead of each signal rather than alongside it. The whole start and pre-taxi sequence needed no repeated exchange. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate ground-crew signal coordination.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated the marshaller's requirements at every step, so no signal was repeated or clarified across the whole start and pre-taxi sequence. The exchange stayed unambiguous and correctly timed from the first switch to the last. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary ground-crew signal coordination.

error_modes.label: TAXI ROUTE ADHERENCE AND OBSTACLE CLEARANCE

texts.0: SP, due to an incomplete read of the taxi clearance before releasing the brakes, did not follow the specified taxi route and did not ensure that the ground path of the A/C was clear of obstacles. SP turned onto the wrong taxiway and continued toward a parked aircraft whose wingtip clearance was not assessed. The IP intervened, took control and stopped the aircraft before the turn was completed.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete read of the taxi clearance before releasing the brakes, did not follow the specified taxi route with certainty. SP started the wrong turn and corrected it only after two verbal indications from the IP that the cleared route was the parallel taxiway. The aircraft rejoined the correct route, but the correction was late and depended entirely on IP prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed identification of the taxiway markings under low light, did not track the specified taxi route on the first turn. SP recognized the discrepancy against the airfield chart within one aircraft length, stopped, and rejoined the cleared route without prompting. The ground path stayed clear of obstacles and no IP intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP followed the specified taxi route throughout and ensured that the ground path of the A/C remained clear of obstacles. SP identified each taxiway and hold point against the airfield chart in advance and kept the aircraft on the marked centerline. The whole taxi was completed without IP intervention or clarification.
texts.4: SP followed the specified taxi route precisely from chocks to the hold point, with the aircraft tracking the taxiway centerline throughout. SP scanned continuously outside for obstacles and wingtip clearance, and identified every turn before reaching it. No correction, prompt or IP input was required at any stage of the taxi.
texts.marginal: SP followed the specified taxi route and kept the ground path clear of obstacles, so the standard was met. However, SP identified the second turn only on reaching it and allowed the aircraft to track slightly off the centerline through that turn, which reduces the margin available on a congested ramp. SP is expected to identify each turn one segment in advance and to keep the nosewheel on the centerline through the turn.

texts_at.0: With the IP reading the taxi clearance aloud and pointing out each turn on the airfield chart, SP steered the aircraft along the route called. The habit of reading the clearance against the chart before releasing the brakes has not yet been built, so turns are still identified as they are reached rather than in advance. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin identifying each turn against the chart before releasing the brakes.
texts_at.1: SP corrected the wrong turn onto the taxiway only after two verbal indications from the IP that the parallel taxiway was the cleared route, because the taxi clearance had not been fully read before the brakes were released. The aircraft rejoined the correct route once the indications were given. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to complete the read of the clearance before releasing the brakes on the next taxi.
texts_at.2: SP recognized a discrepancy against the airfield chart within one aircraft length of the wrong turn and rejoined the cleared route without the IP raising it, after a delayed identification of the taxiway markings under low light. The ground path stayed clear of obstacles throughout. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to identify the taxiway markings earlier so the discrepancy does not develop.
texts_at.3: SP followed the specified taxi route throughout and kept the ground path clear of obstacles, identifying each taxiway and hold point against the airfield chart in advance. The second turn was identified only on reaching it, and the aircraft tracked slightly off the centerline through that turn. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to identify every turn one segment ahead rather than on arrival.

texts_above.1: SP rejoined the correct taxi route, identifying the parallel taxiway as the cleared route. The correction followed two verbal indications from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP tracked the cleared taxi route and kept the ground path clear of obstacles, identifying one taxiway marking late under low light and correcting the track within a single aircraft length without any IP input. The remainder of the taxi followed the airfield chart without further hesitation. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady taxi-route awareness.
texts_above.3: SP identified every taxiway and hold point against the airfield chart in advance and kept the aircraft on the marked centerline for the whole taxi, with no turn identified late. The ground path remained clear of obstacles from chocks to the hold point. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed taxi-route awareness.
texts_above.4: SP scanned continuously for obstacles and wingtip clearance while tracking the taxiway centerline precisely from chocks to the hold point, identifying every turn before reaching it. No correction, prompt or IP input was required at any stage of the taxi. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional taxi-route awareness.

error_modes.label: TAXI SPEED CONTROL, STOPPING AND HOLDING THE AIRCRAFT STATIONARY

texts.0: SP, due to late and abrupt brake application from an excessive taxi speed, did not stop the A/C as required and allowed longitudinal oscillations on each stop. SP overran the hold-short line and, during the leak check, allowed the aircraft to creep forward while the check was still in progress. The IP intervened on the brakes and repositioned the aircraft before the check could be completed.
texts.1: SP, due to late and abrupt brake application from an excessive taxi speed, did not stop the A/C smoothly and stopped short of the hold line only after the IP called for brakes. SP allowed two noticeable pitch oscillations on the final stop and had to be reminded verbally to hold the aircraft stationary for the leak check. The aircraft was eventually held correctly, but only through IP prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a taxi speed slightly above that required for the ramp area, did not achieve a smooth first stop and produced one perceptible pitch oscillation. SP reduced power early for the subsequent stops, and the aircraft was stopped on the line and held completely stationary through the leak check. All corrections were made by SP without any IP intervention.
texts.3: SP stopped the A/C as required, without oscillations and without IP's intervention, using early power reduction and progressive braking. SP held the aircraft completely stationary through the leak check and the line-up, allowing no movement at any point where the aircraft had to be halted. Taxi speed remained appropriate to the ramp and taxiway areas throughout.
texts.4: SP controlled taxi speed precisely and brought the A/C to a stop on the mark each time with no perceptible pitch oscillation. SP held the aircraft absolutely stationary during the leak check and the line-up, with brakes set before the check was called. No IP input, prompt or correction was required at any stage.
texts.marginal: SP stopped the A/C as required and allowed no movement where the aircraft had to be halted, so the standard was met. However, SP's first stop needed a firmer than necessary brake input because power was reduced late, and one slight pitch oscillation was perceptible. SP is expected to plan the deceleration earlier so that braking is progressive and the stop is achieved without any oscillation.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling for the power reduction and the brake application at each stop, SP controlled the taxi speed and the brakes on the calls given. The relationship between taxi speed and the braking needed for a smooth stop has not yet been learned, so power is still reduced on a call rather than in anticipation of the stop. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to begin reducing power for the stop without the call being given.
texts_at.1: SP stopped the A/C short of the hold line only after the IP called for brakes, because the taxi speed into the stop had been slightly excessive and the brake application arrived late and firm. The aircraft was then held stationary correctly for the leak check. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to call for the brake reduction from the taxi speed itself rather than after the IP's prompt.
texts_at.2: SP produced one perceptible pitch oscillation on the first stop from a taxi speed slightly above that required for the ramp area, then reduced power early for the remaining stops and held the aircraft completely stationary through the leak check without IP intervention. Every correction after the first stop was made unprompted. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to reduce taxi speed earlier so the first stop matches the later ones.
texts_at.3: SP stopped the A/C as required, without oscillations and without IP intervention, using early power reduction and progressive braking, and held it completely stationary through the leak check and the line-up. The deceleration on the first stop needed a firmer brake input than the later ones because power was reduced a moment later. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to reduce power at the same point on every stop.

texts_above.1: SP brought the aircraft to a stop and held it stationary for the leak check. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP reduced power early enough to avoid an oscillation on all but the first stop of the taxi, and held the A/C completely stationary through the leak check and the line-up without any IP intervention. The one firmer brake input needed on the first stop did not carry into the deceleration that followed. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound taxi-speed and brake control.
texts_above.3: SP brought the A/C to a stop with early power reduction and progressive braking on every occasion, holding it completely stationary through the leak check and the line-up with no oscillation at any point. Taxi speed stayed matched to the ramp and taxiway areas throughout. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise taxi-speed and brake control.
texts_above.4: SP controlled taxi speed so precisely that every stop landed on the mark with no perceptible pitch oscillation, holding the aircraft absolutely stationary for the leak check with brakes set before the check was called. No IP input, prompt or correction was required at any stage. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding taxi-speed and brake control.

error_modes.label: KNOWLEDGE AND CORRECT USE OF A/C LEVERS AND SWITCHES

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient cockpit familiarity with the switch panel layout, did not know and did not use correctly all A/C levers and switches. SP selected the adjacent switch on two occasions and left one system in the wrong configuration after the check was called complete. The IP intervened, identified the mis-selections and reconfigured the affected systems before taxi.
texts.1: SP, due to insufficient cockpit familiarity with the switch panel layout, did not select the correct switch on the first attempt for three items of the ground flow. SP corrected each one only after the IP pointed out the discrepancy, and required a direct indication of the switch location on two of them. The final configuration was correct, but it was achieved through IP direction rather than by SP.
texts.2: SP, due to hesitation in locating two less frequently used switches, did not operate them within the flow rhythm required by the check list. SP identified the correct control on the second look, selected it and verified the corresponding indication before continuing. All levers and switches ended in the correct position without any IP intervention.
texts.3: SP knew and used correctly all A/C levers and switches, selecting each control on the first attempt and verifying the associated indication. SP applied the correct technique on the guarded and detented controls without needing to search for them. The ground configuration was complete and correct with no IP input.
texts.4: SP operated every A/C lever and switch correctly, without hesitation and with the associated indication confirmed each time. SP's hand went directly to each control, including the less frequently used ones, and the flow rhythm was unbroken from Before Start through Before Taxi. No mis-selection, search or IP prompt occurred at any point.
texts.marginal: SP knew and used correctly all A/C levers and switches and the final configuration was accurate, so the standard was met. However, SP had to search visually for two of the less frequently used controls, which broke the flow rhythm and would cost time under a compressed sequence. SP is expected to consolidate the switch locations by touch so that selection keeps pace with the check list.

texts_at.0: With the IP pointing to each lever and switch in turn and naming the required position, SP selected the controls named on the early repetitions of the flow. The switch panel layout has not yet been learned well enough to select from memory, so each control is still found by being pointed to rather than by habit. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin selecting the more frequently used switches without them being pointed to.
texts_at.1: SP corrected the mis-selected switch and reconfigured the affected system only after the IP pointed out the discrepancy and gave a direct indication of its location, because cockpit familiarity with the panel layout was still developing. The final configuration was correct once the indication had been given. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to select the correct switch on the first attempt without needing the location pointed out.
texts_at.2: SP identified the correct control on the second look for two less frequently used switches and verified the corresponding indication before continuing, with no IP intervention needed at any point. All levers and switches ended in the correct position. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to reduce the search to a single look by learning the less frequent switch locations.
texts_at.3: SP knew and used correctly all A/C levers and switches, selecting each control on the first attempt and verifying the associated indication, applying the correct technique on the guarded and detented controls without searching. The flow rhythm slowed briefly on the two least frequently used switches even though each was selected correctly. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring the flow rhythm on those two switches up to the pace of the rest of the check.

texts_above.1: SP corrected the switch selections and reached the correct final configuration on all three items of the ground flow. The correction followed the IP pointing out the discrepancy on each one. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP selected every A/C lever and switch correctly, needing a second look for only one of the less frequently used controls before verifying its indication, with no IP intervention at any point. The ground configuration was complete and correct at the end of the flow. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable cockpit switch knowledge.
texts_above.3: SP selected each control on the first attempt and verified the associated indication throughout the ground flow, including the guarded and detented controls that are not searched for by habit. No switch selection broke the flow rhythm at any point. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good cockpit switch knowledge.
texts_above.4: SP's hand went directly to every control, including the less frequently used ones, with the flow rhythm unbroken from Before Start through Before Taxi and no mis-selection or search at any point. The associated indication was confirmed each time without a pause. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior cockpit switch knowledge.

error_modes.label: NAVIGATION AIDS AND GPS SETUP AND OPERATION

texts.0: SP, due to mode confusion over the selected avionics mode and what it was protecting, did not demonstrate knowledge of the use and operation of the A/C navigation aids and the GPS. SP left the navigation source on the wrong selection and loaded a flight plan that did not match the briefed instrument departure. The IP intervened, corrected the navigation source and reloaded the flight plan before taxi was authorized.
texts.1: SP, due to mode confusion over the selected avionics mode and what it was protecting, did not set the navigation aids and the GPS to the configuration required by the briefed instrument profile. SP identified the wrong navigation source only after three verbal indications from the IP and needed direction to sequence the GPS flight plan correctly. The setup was completed accurately but entirely under IP guidance.
texts.2: SP, due to an incorrect first assumption about which navigation mode was active, did not couple the display to the intended source at the first attempt. SP cross-checked the selection against the briefed departure, recognized the mismatch and reselected the correct source and GPS leg before taxi. The navigation setup was completed correctly with no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP demonstrated knowledge of the use and operation of the A/C navigation aids and the GPS, setting each source, frequency and course to the values required by the briefed instrument profile. SP verified the active GPS leg and the identification of each tuned aid before taxi. The complete navigation setup was accomplished without IP input.
texts.4: SP set and verified the A/C navigation aids and the GPS accurately and without hesitation, with every frequency, course and mode matching the briefed instrument departure. SP identified each aid, confirmed the active GPS leg and stated the expected first indications before taxi. The setup required no correction, repetition or IP involvement of any kind.
texts.marginal: SP set the navigation aids and the GPS correctly for the briefed profile and knew their operation, so the standard was met. However, SP reached the correct GPS page through two intermediate selections and confirmed the active mode only when asked to state it, which shows the mode logic is not yet fully consolidated. SP is expected to reach the required page directly and to state the active navigation source without being prompted.

texts_at.0: With the IP naming the active avionics mode and demonstrating the GPS sequence, SP set the navigation aids and the GPS to the values given. The avionics mode logic has not yet been learned well enough to identify independently, so the active mode is still confirmed by the IP rather than tested by SP. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin testing the assumed mode against the briefed departure without it being named.
texts_at.1: SP identified the correct navigation source and sequenced the GPS flight plan only after three verbal indications from the IP, because an incorrect first assumption about the active avionics mode had been carried into the setup. The configuration was accurate once the indications had been followed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to test the assumed mode against the briefed departure before acting on it.
texts_at.2: SP cross-checked the navigation selection against the briefed departure, recognized a mismatch from an incorrect first assumption about the active mode and reselected the correct source and GPS leg before taxi, without any IP intervention. The setup was completed correctly before the departure request. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to verify the active mode before the first selection rather than after.
texts_at.3: SP demonstrated knowledge of the use and operation of the navigation aids and the GPS, setting each source, frequency and course to the values required by the briefed instrument profile and verifying the active leg before taxi. texts_above.3: SP set every navigation source, frequency and course to the values the briefed instrument profile required and verified the active GPS leg and the identification of each tuned aid before taxi, with no mode assumption left unchecked. error_modes.label: INTERROGATION AND COORDINATION WITH THE IP ON PROCEDURES

texts.0: SP, due to an unstated request for a repeat of the instruction that was not understood, did not ask and did not wait for the IP's answer about the (BOTH) procedures. SP proceeded on an assumption that contradicted the briefed sequence and configured the aircraft accordingly. The IP intervened, stopped the action and re-briefed the procedure on the ground before the flow could continue.
texts.1: SP, due to an unstated request for a repeat of the instruction that was not understood, did not raise the ambiguity in the (BOTH) procedures at the point where it arose. SP acted on the assumption and clarified it only after two direct questions from the IP about what had been understood. The procedure was completed correctly, but the coordination was initiated by the IP rather than by SP.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed decision to voice a point that was not fully clear, did not ask about the (BOTH) procedures at the moment the doubt appeared. SP held the action, asked the question before any switch was moved and waited for the IP's answer before proceeding. The sequence continued correctly and no IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP asked about the (BOTH) procedures and waited for the IP's answer before acting, keeping the exchange short and specific. SP stated clearly what was understood and confirmed the agreed sequence before continuing the ground flow. The coordination was complete and left no mis-apprehension between the cockpits.
texts.4: SP raised every point of the (BOTH) procedures that required confirmation, asked precisely and waited for the IP's answer each time before acting. SP's questions anticipated the ambiguity rather than following it, so the sequence was agreed in advance and never had to be interrupted. Coordination between the cockpits remained complete throughout the ground phase.
texts.marginal: SP asked about the (BOTH) procedures and waited for the IP's answer, so the standard was met. However, the question was raised late in the sequence and phrased tentatively, and SP had already begun reaching for the control before the answer was given. SP is expected to state the doubt as soon as it arises and to keep hands clear until the IP's answer has been received.

texts_at.0: With the IP prompting SP to state what was understood about the (BOTH) procedures, SP answered the direct questions asked. The habit of raising a doubt at the moment it appears has not yet been built, so an unclear point is still acted on by assumption until the IP asks about it. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to begin raising a doubt at the moment it appears without the IP asking first.

SP is expected to raise the doubt at the moment it appears rather than acting on an assumption first.
texts_at.2: SP held the action, asked about the (BOTH) procedures before any switch was moved and waited for the IP's answer, after a delayed decision to voice a point that was not fully clear. The sequence continued correctly and no IP intervention was required. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to voice the point as soon as it appears rather than after a pause.
texts_at.3: SP asked about the (BOTH) procedures and waited for the IP's answer before acting, stating clearly what was understood and confirming the agreed sequence, and left no mis-apprehension between the cockpits. The question was raised a little later in the sequence than the doubt itself had appeared. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to raise the question at the first moment the doubt is felt.

texts_above.1: SP clarified the ambiguity in the (BOTH) procedures and completed the action correctly. The correction followed two direct questions from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP asked about the (BOTH) procedures and waited for the IP's answer before acting, holding the switch action until the point that had been unclear was resolved, without the IP needing to prompt the question. The sequence then continued correctly with no further doubt. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good cockpit coordination on procedures.
texts_above.3: SP raised every point of the (BOTH) procedures that needed confirmation and waited for the IP's answer before acting, keeping each exchange short and specific and leaving no mis-apprehension between the cockpits. The coordination stayed complete through the whole ground flow. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate cockpit coordination on procedures.
texts_above.4: SP's questions anticipated the ambiguity in the (BOTH) procedures rather than following it, so the sequence was agreed in advance and never had to be interrupted once the ground flow was under way. Coordination between the cockpits remained complete throughout. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary cockpit coordination on procedures.

error_modes.label: IFR CLEARANCE COPY AND CHADS ORGANIZATION

texts.0: SP, due to expecting the ATC clearance to mirror exactly what was filed on the flight plan form, did not copy the clearance in an organized CHADS format and did not detect the elements ATC had changed. SP left the departure frequency and the squawk blank and read back the filed routing after ATC had amended it. The IP intervened, took the radio, requested a full re-read of the clearance and had it copied again before the taxi request.
texts.1: SP, due to expecting the clearance to mirror the filed flight plan, did not organize the copy under the CHADS headings and lost two of the five elements while writing. SP asked ATC for a full repetition twice and still needed three verbal indications from the IP to enter the assigned altitude and squawk in the right places. The clearance was finally complete and read back correctly, but only under continuous IP direction.
texts.2: SP, due to writing the clearance as continuous text instead of filling the CHADS blocks, did not have the departure frequency and the squawk separated when the read back was due. SP recognized the gap before keying the transmitter, requested one repetition on own initiative and completed the CHADS blocks. The read back was accepted by ATC at the first attempt and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP copied the ATC clearance under the CHADS headings, filling clearance limit, heading, altitude, departure frequency and squawk as each was passed. SP compared the copied clearance against the filed route, identified the amended routing and read the whole clearance back correctly at the first attempt. The airfield diagram was reviewed before the taxi request without IP input.
texts.4: SP copied the ATC clearance directly into the CHADS blocks with no gaps and no request for repetition, and read it back verbatim at the first attempt. SP stated aloud which element differed from the filed flight plan and confirmed the amended routing against the approach plate before the taxi request. The whole clearance sequence was completed with no correction and no IP involvement of any kind.
texts.marginal: SP copied the clearance completely and the read back was accepted by ATC at the first attempt, so the standard was met. However SP filled the CHADS blocks out of sequence and needed a few seconds to locate the assigned squawk when the IP asked for it, which shows the format is not yet automatic under radio pace. SP is expected to fill each CHADS block as the element is passed and to be able to state any of them immediately on request.

texts_at.0: With the IP naming each CHADS heading as the clearance was read and pointing out the block to fill, SP wrote the elements called. The CHADS format has not yet been learned well enough to organize a clearance under it in real time, so the copy is still made as continuous text until the IP directs the blocks. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin opening the CHADS blocks before copying without them being pointed to.
texts_at.1: SP entered the assigned altitude and squawk in the CHADS blocks only after three verbal indications from the IP, because the clearance had been copied as continuous text rather than under the CHADS headings. The clearance was read back correctly once the blocks had been completed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to open the CHADS blocks before copying rather than after the read-back is due.
texts_at.2: SP recognized that the departure frequency and squawk had not been separated when the read back was due, requested one repetition on own initiative and completed the CHADS blocks before transmitting, with no IP input. The read back was accepted by ATC on the first attempt. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to fill the blocks as each element is passed so no repetition is needed.
texts_at.3: SP copied the ATC clearance under the CHADS headings, comparing it against the filed route and reading the whole clearance back correctly on the first attempt. The CHADS blocks were filled slightly out of sequence, and a few seconds were needed to locate the assigned squawk when it was asked for. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to fill each block as its element is passed so any of them can be stated immediately.

texts_above.1: SP completed the CHADS blocks and read the clearance back correctly. The correction followed three verbal indications from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP filled the CHADS blocks as the clearance was passed and compared the copy against the filed route, catching one gap in the departure frequency before the read back was due and closing it without IP input. The clearance was read back correctly on the first attempt. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent CHADS clearance-copy technique.
texts_above.3: SP filled clearance limit, heading, altitude, departure frequency and squawk into the CHADS blocks as each was passed, identified the amended routing against the filed flight plan and read the whole clearance back correctly on the first attempt. The airfield diagram was reviewed before the taxi request with no IP input. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed CHADS clearance-copy technique.
texts_above.4: SP copied the ATC clearance directly into the CHADS blocks with no gaps and no request for repetition, read it back verbatim on the first attempt and stated aloud which element differed from the filed flight plan. The whole clearance sequence was completed with no correction of any kind. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional CHADS clearance-copy technique.

error_modes.label: INSTRUMENT COCKPIT ORGANIZATION: CHARTS, PLATES AND RMU STANDBY FREQUENCY

texts.0: SP, due to leaving the additional instrument publications unprepared instead of prefolding them and storing them in the order of use, did not have an organized cockpit setup for the planned instrument sortie. SP boarded with unfolded charts, no tabs on the approach plates and the departure plate buried under the IFR supplement. The IP intervened, stopped the flow before start and had the publications refolded, tabbed and re-stowed in order of use.
texts.1: SP, due to prefolding only part of the instrument publications, did not store the charts and approach plates in the order in which they would be used. SP could not produce the departure plate when it was called for and needed three verbal indications from the IP to tab the required pages and to write down the frequencies as they were assigned. The cockpit was eventually organized, but every step was directed by the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to stowing the approach plates by airfield rather than in the order of use, did not have the departure plate on top when the clearance was copied. SP recognized the disorder while still in uncongested parking, re-sequenced the plates, tabbed the required pages and wrote down the assigned frequencies. The cockpit was organized in time for taxi and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP prefolded all charts before strap in and stored the publications in the order in which they would be used, with the required pages of the IFR supplement and the approach plates marked by tabs. SP wrote down each radio frequency as it was assigned and used the RMU standby frequency function to anticipate the next change. The instrument cockpit setup was completed without IP input.
texts.4: SP arrived with every chart prefolded, every required plate tabbed and the whole set stowed in exact order of use, with the mission card annotated with the information likely to be needed in flight. SP wrote down each frequency as assigned and preset the next one in the RMU standby window before it was requested. The setup required no rearrangement, no search and no IP involvement of any kind.
texts.marginal: SP had the publications prefolded, tabbed and stowed in order of use and the required pages were available, so the standard was met. However SP loaded the RMU standby frequency only after the change was passed rather than in anticipation, and needed a second look to find the marked page in the IFR supplement. SP is expected to preset the standby frequency ahead of the change and to reach any tabbed page at the first attempt.

texts_at.0: With the IP naming each publication to prefold and pointing to the page to tab, SP prepared the cockpit on the sequence given. The order in which the instrument publications will be used has not yet been learned, so the set is still organized on direction rather than from memory of the sequence. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to begin prefolding and tabbing the full set from memory without the sequence being given.
texts_at.1: SP produced the departure plate and tabbed the required pages only after three verbal indications from the IP, because the instrument publications had been prefolded only in part before strap in. The cockpit was organized correctly once the indications had been given. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to prefold and tab every required publication before strap in rather than part of the set.
texts_at.2: SP recognized that the approach plates had been stowed by airfield rather than by order of use, re-sequenced them, tabbed the required pages and wrote down the assigned frequencies while still in uncongested parking, with no IP input. The cockpit was organized in time for taxi. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to stow the plates in order of use from the start so no re-sequencing is needed.

The RMU standby frequency was loaded only after the change was passed rather than in anticipation of it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to preset the standby frequency ahead of the change on the next sortie.

The cockpit was organized in time for taxi. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid cockpit organization of charts and plates.
texts_above.3: SP stored every chart and approach plate in the exact order of use with the required IFR supplement pages tabbed, and wrote down each radio frequency as it was assigned. The RMU standby frequency function was used to anticipate the next change on every occasion.
